acceptedAnswer.text: A custom-made occlusal splint, often called a night guard, is a clinically recognised protective measure for patients with bruxism. The splint is worn over the teeth during sleep and acts as a barrier between the upper and lower teeth, absorbing and distributing grinding forces before they can damage the composite.
In some cases, a dentist may recommend minor adjustments to the bite to reduce uneven pressure on specific teeth or bonded areas. This is assessed and carried out on an individual basis.

Scheduling regular dental check-ups allows the condition of composite restorations to be monitored over time. Early identification of wear or minor damage may allow for prompt repair before more significant issues develop.

Bruxism can sometimes be related to stress, sleep disorders, or other factors. Addressing these underlying causes — whether through lifestyle adjustments, relaxation techniques, or medical referral — may help reduce the frequency or intensity of grinding over time.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding last if I grind my teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of composite bonding varies considerably between patients and depends on many individual factors, including the severity of bruxism, the location of the bonded teeth, and whether protective measures such as a night guard are used. In patients without grinding, composite bonding may last several years with good care. In patients with unmanaged bruxism, longevity may be reduced. A dentist can give you a realistic expectation based on your individual clinical situation during a consultation.

mainEntity.name: Will my dentist refuse composite bonding if I have bruxism?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. A dentist will assess the extent of your bruxism and discuss the risks and protective options with you before making a clinical recommendation. In many cases, composite bonding can be provided alongside an occlusal splint to help manage the impact of grinding. The decision is made on an individual basis, taking into account the overall clinical picture, your preferences, and a transparent discussion of likely outcomes.

mainEntity.name: Can grinding cause composite bonding to fall off completely?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, severe or prolonged grinding can lead to debonding — where the composite resin separates from the tooth surface. This is more likely if bruxism is unmanaged and no protective splint is worn. Regular dental check-ups help to detect early signs of stress on the bonding before complete loss occurs. If a bonded section does become loose or falls away, it is advisable to contact a dental practice promptly for assessment and repair.

mainEntity.name: Is composite bonding or porcelain veneers better for bruxism patients?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both composite bonding and porcelain veneers have their respective advantages and limitations in the context of bruxism. Porcelain is generally harder and more resistant to surface wear than composite resin, but it can be more brittle and may cause wear to opposing teeth if grinding forces are high. Composite bonding, while less wear-resistant, can be more easily repaired if damage occurs. The most suitable option depends on the individual patient's clinical situation and should be discussed in detail with a dental professional.

mainEntity.name: Can teeth grinding damage natural teeth as well as composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Bruxism can cause significant damage to natural tooth structure over time, including enamel erosion, tooth fractures, increased sensitivity, and changes to the bite. This is one reason why managing bruxism is important for overall oral health, independent of whether a patient has cosmetic restorations. A dentist can assess the condition of both natural teeth and any restorations during a clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I notice my composite bonding has chipped?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you notice that your composite bonding has chipped, cracked, or changed in appearance, it is advisable to contact your dental practice to arrange an assessment. Minor chips can often be repaired relatively straightforwardly by adding and reshaping composite resin. It is also a good opportunity to discuss whether bruxism may be contributing to the damage and whether a night guard or other protective measures would be beneficial going forward.
